subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Show that the circles x² + y² − 6x − 2y + 1 = 0 and x² + y² + 2x − 8y + 13 = 0 touch each other. Find the point of contact and the equation of the common tangent at their point of contact.

mark_split.label: Centre and radius of the first circle
Centre and radius of the second circle

insider_note: Two separate facts decide everything: C₁C₂ = r₁ + r₂ means external touching, and external touching means the point of contact divides C₁C₂ INTERNALLY in the ratio r₁ : r₂ — the wording is the opposite of what most students expect and is where the marks are lost.

steps.label: Centre and radius of the first circle
steps.margin_note: One mark. Read g and f as half the coefficients of x and y, then change the sign for the centre.
steps.memory_tip: Centre is (−g, −f) and radius is √(g² + f² − c). Halve, then flip the sign.
steps.why: Comparing with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 gives 2g = −6 and 2f = −2, so g = −3 and f = −1. The centre is (−g, −f) and the radius is √(g² + f² − c).
common_mistakes: Writing the centre as (−3, −1) by forgetting the second sign change.

steps.label: Centre and radius of the second circle
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both radii come out whole here, which is the sign that the numbers in the question were chosen to touch.
steps.memory_tip: Do the two circles the same way, one under the other, so the comparison later is easy to read.
steps.why: The same reading gives the second centre and radius. Both radii are whole numbers, so the touching test that follows will be exact rather than approximate.
common_mistakes: Computing √(1 + 16 + 13) by taking c as +13 with the wrong sign in the formula.

steps.label: Show that the circles touch
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Say WHICH kind of touching: C₁C₂ = r₁ + r₂ is external, C₁C₂ = |r₁ − r₂| is internal.
steps.memory_tip: Sum of the radii equals the distance between the centres: the circles are outside each other and meet at one point.
lines: ∴ The circles touch each other externally.
steps.why: If the distance between the centres equals the sum of the radii, the two circles meet at exactly one point and each lies outside the other. If it equalled the difference, one would lie inside the other.
common_mistakes: Showing only that the circles meet, without naming external or internal touching.
Comparing C₁C₂ with r₁ − r₂ and concluding they do not touch.

steps.label: Find the point of contact
steps.margin_note: Two marks. External touching uses the INTERNAL division formula — the point of contact lies between the centres.
steps.memory_tip: The contact point is between the centres, so it divides C₁C₂ internally in the ratio r₁ : r₂.
lines: The point of contact P lies on C₁C₂ and
divides it internally in the ratio 3 : 2
steps.why: For circles touching externally the contact point sits on the segment joining the centres, at distance r₁ from C₁ and r₂ from C₂. That is exactly internal division in the ratio r₁ : r₂.
common_mistakes: Writing the ratio as r₂ : r₁ and swapping the two centres in the formula.

steps.label: Find the common tangent
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Subtract the two equations exactly as written; the x² and y² terms must vanish.
steps.memory_tip: The common tangent at the point of contact is simply S − S′ = 0.
lines: The common tangent at the point of contact
steps.why: Both circles have the same x² and y² terms, so S − S′ = 0 is a straight line. When the circles touch, that line meets both of them only at the contact point, so it is the common tangent there. A check: 4(3/5) − 3(14/5) + 6 = (12 − 42 + 30)/5 = 0, so P lies on it.
common_mistakes: Subtracting only some of the terms and leaving an x² behind.
Dividing by −2 and keeping the signs of the original line.

steps.label: The picture
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own; the question does not ask for a diagram. Draw it in rough to decide internal or external division before writing the section formula.
steps.memory_tip: Sketch the two circles side by side. The contact point sits between the centres, so the division is internal.
steps.why: The picture settles the one decision that carries the marks. With the circles drawn outside each other, P is plainly between C₁ and C₂, so the section formula must be the internal one, and the common tangent is the line through P at right angles to C₁C₂.
common_mistakes: Drawing one circle inside the other, which leads to external division and a wrong point.
Drawing the tangent through a centre instead of through the contact point.
